strengths: Well-motivated design grounded in cognitive science (working memory + hippocampal episodic memory), translated into a concrete and technically coherent architecture (perceptual/cognitive tokens, retrieval via cross-attention with timestep PE, gated fusion, and similarity-based consolidation).

Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 3 robots, 10 suites, 150+ tasks, 500+ variations spanning SimplerEnv-Bridge, SimplerEnv-Fractal, LIBERO (5 suites), and 12 real-world tasks on Franka and WidowX, which is unusually comprehensive for this line of work.

Consistent and often substantial improvements over strong, recent baselines (CogACT, π0, SpatialVLA, OpenVLA, TraceVLA, RoboVLMs, Magma), including large gains specifically on tasks designed to require temporal reasoning (e.g., +26 on real-world long-horizon tasks, +14.6 on Bridge), supporting the core claim that memory helps non-Markovian manipulation.

Solid ablation studies isolating the contributions of memory type (perceptual vs cognitive vs both), memory length, timestep positional encoding, gating fusion vs addition, and token-merge vs FIFO consolidation, with consistent directionality supporting design choices.

Extensive robustness/generalization analysis under real and simulated OOD conditions (backgrounds, distractors, lighting, objects, containers, occlusion, camera views), which is valuable and often missing in competing VLA papers.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, training data descriptions, data augmentation, evaluation protocols, and qualitative rollouts provided in appendix.
weaknesses: The cognitive science framing (working memory vs. hippocampal verbatim/gist memory) is largely a loose analogy/narrative rather than a rigorously derived mechanism; the actual memory bank (cross-attention retrieval + gating + cosine-similarity merging) is a fairly standard memory-augmented transformer design also seen in video/robotics memory literature (e.g., RMem, RoboFlamingo, TraceVLA), so novelty over these lies mainly in combining perceptual+cognitive streams rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Memory length ablation only tested on SimplerEnv-Bridge (single suite) with 4/16/64, and the real-world Long-horizon Temporal suite reportedly uses memory length 256 without ablation or justification for why such a large jump is needed or how performance scales with it.

No analysis of computational/inference overhead (latency, memory footprint) introduced by the PCMB and retrieval/consolidation steps relative to baselines like CogACT/π0, which matters for real-time robotic control claims.

Reported baselines for π0 in Table 1/2 are reproduced from a third-party repo (open-pi-zero) with different input modalities (proprioception) and sampling strategies, and some VA settings are simply missing for π0, making some comparisons only partially apples-to-apples; similarly π0/π0-FAST in LIBERO use extra wrist-camera and proprioceptive inputs while MemoryVLA does not, which is acknowledged but complicates strict fairness claims of 'outperforming state-of-the-art' uniformly.

Some ablations (Tab 5/6) are conducted only on SimplerEnv-Bridge; it is unclear whether the same design choices (e.g., memory length=16, gate fusion, token merge) generalize optimally to LIBERO or real-world long-horizon tasks with much longer horizons, given the very different memory length used there (256) without further ablation.

The paper claims 'non-Markovian' motivation via the Push Buttons example, but no controlled ablation isolates how much of the improvement stems from memory vs. simply a stronger diffusion action-expert backbone/architecture compared to baselines (CogACT also uses diffusion head), leaving some residual ambiguity about attribution of gains purely to the memory mechanism versus other architectural differences (e.g., DiT design, VLM backbone choice).

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in VLA research: modeling non-Markovian temporal dependencies in robotic manipulation, motivated by a clear cognitive-science analogy (working memory vs. episodic memory).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 150+ tasks and 500+ variations across 3 robots and 6 benchmarks (SimplerEnv-Bridge/Fractal, LIBERO, Mikasa-Robo, and 12 real-world tasks), which is unusually thorough for this line of work.

Consistent and often large improvements over strong, recent baselines (CogACT, π0, SpatialVLA, CronusVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, etc.) across nearly all benchmarks, including substantial gains (+14.6 Bridge, +11.8 Mikasa-Robo, +26 real-world long-horizon), lending credibility to the claimed benefits of the memory mechanism.

Well-designed ablations isolating the contributions of memory type (perceptual vs. cognitive vs. both), memory length, retrieval (timestep PE), fusion (gate vs. add), and consolidation (token merge vs. FIFO), which support the architectural design choices.

Extensive appendix material including inference efficiency analysis (showing minimal overhead, ~3.6% latency increase), robustness/OOD generalization tests, zero-shot task generalization, comparisons against additional temporal-context VLA baselines (TraceVLA, RoboVLMs, CronusVLA, 4D-VLA, TTF-VLA, MAP-VLA), and qualitative case studies visualizing memory retrieval attention patterns.

The proposed Perceptual-Cognitive Memory Bank with retrieval/fusion/consolidation is a reasonably novel and well-motivated mechanism compared to prior simpler temporal approaches (LSTM latent propagation in RoboFlamingo, trajectory painting in TraceVLA, prompt-based history in UniVLA).
weaknesses: Some baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: e.g., π0/π0-FAST use additional proprioceptive and wrist-camera inputs while MemoryVLA uses only third-person RGB, which could partly explain relative gains/losses and complicates fair attribution of improvements solely to the memory mechanism.

The zero-shot task generalization experiment (Appendix I) is very small-scale (5 trials per task) and shows notably degraded performance (avg 0.47 on OOD tasks vs 0.8 on base task), suggesting the memory mechanism's benefits may not generalize as strongly to novel task semantics as the paper's framing might suggest.

Robustness results show a substantial performance drop under unseen camera views (e.g., Pick Coke Can drops from 92% to 42%), which is a notable weakness only briefly acknowledged rather than analyzed in depth.

The real-world evaluation, while extensive in task diversity, uses relatively small trial counts (10-15 trials for long-horizon tasks) which limits statistical confidence in the large reported margins (e.g., +26 points).

Memory consolidation via similarity-based merging of adjacent entries is a simple heuristic (greedy pairwise cosine similarity merge) that may not scale well or generalize to more complex/longer real-world temporal horizons beyond what was tested, and its interaction with very long real-world temporal memory (256+ length) is only lightly ablated.

The paper's presentation is heavily weighted toward extensive quantitative results, but deeper analysis of failure cases (beyond brief OOD discussion) and theoretical justification for specific design choices (e.g., why merge only the single most similar adjacent pair rather than more principled memory management) is limited.

strengths: Extremely extensive empirical evaluation: 3 robots, 6 benchmarks (SimplerEnv-Bridge/Fractal, LIBERO's 5 suites, Mikasa-Robo), and 12 real-world tasks spanning general and long-horizon temporal categories, totaling 150+ tasks with 500+ variations.

Consistent and often substantial performance gains over strong, recent baselines (CogACT, π0, SpatialVLA, OpenVLA) across nearly all benchmarks, with particularly large improvements on memory-dependent tasks (Mikasa-Robo, long-horizon real-world tasks).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of memory type (perceptual vs. cognitive vs. both), memory length, retrieval positional encoding, gating fusion vs. addition, and token-merge vs. FIFO consolidation, with some ablations extended to LIBERO-90 and real-world tasks in the appendix.
Inference efficiency analysis shows the memory module adds negligible latency/memory overhead (~4-5%) relative to a non-memory baseline, suggesting practical deployability.

Robustness/generalization experiments under real-world and simulated OOD conditions (background, lighting, distractors, occlusion, camera view) provide some evidence of practical resilience, and additional temporal-context VLA baselines (TraceVLA, RoboVLMs, CronusVLA, TTF-VLA, 4D-VLA, MAP-VLA) were added for fairer comparison in the appendix.

The perceptual-cognitive dual-memory design is a reasonably clean architectural instantiation of a cognitive-science-inspired hypothesis, and the paper provides qualitative visualizations (memory retrieval attention maps) that offer some interpretability.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is largely incremental: the individual mechanisms (cross-attention memory retrieval with timestep positional encoding, sigmoid gate fusion, similarity-based token merging/consolidation) are well-established techniques from memory-augmented networks and video object segmentation (e.g., RMem, cited by the authors); the main contribution is largely the combination and application to VLA rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Zero-shot task generalization results (Appendix I) are weak, with average OOD success dropping to only 0.47 on unseen but closely related tasks, raising concerns that the strong in-distribution gains may partly reflect overfitting to task-specific memory patterns rather than genuinely robust temporal reasoning.

Baseline comparisons have fairness concerns: π0 numbers on Bridge/Fractal are taken from a third-party reproduction (open-pi-zero) that uses additional proprioceptive inputs and different timestep sampling, CogACT-Large was re-evaluated by the authors themselves, and LIBERO baselines mix methods with extra modalities (wrist camera, proprioception) against a model using only third-person RGB — while acknowledged, this heterogeneity complicates a clean apples-to-apples reading of the headline numbers.

Real-world long-horizon evaluation uses only 10-15 trials per task, which is a small sample size for the large reported margins (e.g., +43, +38 points), raising questions about statistical significance and variance of the results.

The real-world comparison only benchmarks against OpenVLA, π0, and CogACT, omitting comparison with other memory/temporal-context methods discussed extensively in the related work (RoboFlamingo, TraceVLA, UniVLA, Octo, RoboVLMs) in the actual real-robot setting where the paper's core claims about temporal modeling are most tested.

The memory consolidation heuristic (merge the single most-similar adjacent pair when capacity is exceeded) is simplistic and its scalability/robustness for much longer deployments beyond the tested horizons is not analyzed.

Ablations for the core memory design choices are performed almost exclusively on SimplerEnv-Bridge (a relatively simple, short-horizon benchmark), with only limited additional ablations on LIBERO-90/real-world temporal tasks; a more systematic ablation on the actual long-horizon temporal benchmarks that motivate the paper would be more convincing.

Reported '150+ tasks' aggregates many small, templated benchmark task variants (e.g., single-instruction SimplerEnv-Bridge tasks, LIBERO suites), which somewhat inflates the apparent scope of evaluation relative to genuinely distinct manipulation skills.

strengths: Extremely extensive empirical evaluation spanning 3 robots, 6 benchmarks (SimplerEnv-Bridge, SimplerEnv-Fractal, LIBERO, Mikasa-Robo, and two real-world suites), 150+ tasks and 500+ variations, which is unusually thorough for VLA research.

Consistent and often substantial improvements over strong, recent baselines (CogACT, π0, SpatialVLA, OpenVLA) across nearly every benchmark, with particularly large gains on tasks that are explicitly non-Markovian/long-horizon (e.g., +26 points on real-world long-horizon temporal tasks, +11.8 on Mikasa-Robo, +14.6 on SimplerEnv-Bridge), which directly supports the paper's central claim that temporal memory matters.

Well-motivated architecture grounded in cognitive science (working memory vs. hippocampal episodic memory, verbatim vs. gist representations), translated into a concrete and technically clear mechanism (perceptual/cognitive memory streams, cross-attention retrieval with temporal positional encoding, gated fusion, similarity-based consolidation).

Thorough ablation studies (memory type, memory length, retrieval with/without positional encoding, fusion strategy, consolidation strategy) validating each architectural design choice, extended in the appendix to additional benchmarks (real-world temporal task and LIBERO-90) for robustness of the ablation conclusions.

Extensive supplementary analyses beyond the core results: inference efficiency comparison showing the memory module adds negligible latency/memory overhead, real-world and simulated OOD robustness/generalization studies, qualitative case studies of memory retrieval showing interpretable attention over historically relevant frames, zero-shot task generalization, and comparisons against contemporaneous temporal-context VLA baselines (CronusVLA, TraceVLA, RoboVLMs, TTF-VLA, 4D-VLA, MAP-VLA).

Uses only a single third-person RGB frame without wrist cameras or proprioception, yet still outperforms several baselines that use additional modalities, suggesting the gains are attributable to the memory design rather than richer sensory inputs.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: the core components (cross-attention retrieval from a bank, gated fusion, cosine-similarity-based token merging, diffusion action head) are individually well-established techniques recombined for this application; the main contribution is engineering integration and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Ablations for the core design decisions (Tab. 6, 7) are conducted primarily on a single benchmark/suite (SimplerEnv-Bridge) with only 4 tasks, and only partially extended to other settings in the appendix; broader ablation coverage (e.g., LIBERO-Object/Goal, Mikasa-Robo) would strengthen generality claims.

Some baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: CogACT-Large numbers on SimplerEnv-Bridge were re-evaluated by the authors themselves (original paper only reported CogACT-Base), and it is unclear whether identical evaluation protocols/hyperparameters were used; similarly, some baselines use additional proprioceptive/wrist-camera inputs, complicating direct comparison despite the authors' framing.

Absolute performance on Mikasa-Robo remains modest (41.2% average success) despite being state-of-the-art, and the zero-shot task generalization experiment (Appendix I) shows fairly weak results (0.47 average success on OOD tasks with only 5 trials each), suggesting the memory bank may not generalize as robustly to novel task semantics as to temporal dependencies within trained task distributions.

Memory consolidation via simple adjacent-pair cosine-similarity merging is a fairly naive heuristic; its behavior/scalability at very long horizons (beyond the tested 256-step real-world memory length) is not deeply analyzed, and no comparison is made to more principled memory compression/eviction strategies beyond FIFO.

The paper reports strong quantitative gains but offers relatively limited analysis of failure cases or scenarios where the memory mechanism might introduce noise/distraction (e.g., retrieving irrelevant historical context), which would help calibrate the robustness of the claimed benefits.

Reproducibility artifacts (code, model weights, logs, videos) are referenced only as placeholders in the reproducibility statement without actual links provided in this version, making it currently impossible to verify reproducibility claims.
